newsitem.title: UK: Union to stop proprietary trading.
newsitem.headline: Union to stop proprietary trading.

text.p: British financial services and trading group Union Plc said on Tuesday it would be withdrawing from proprietary trading businesses.

It said in a statement that it had advised the Bank of England that it "will no longer wish to enjoy a money market counterparty relationship with them under their new arrangements commencing on March 3, 1997."
Union said that it will run out outstanding positions in the next few weeks.

Union warned in January that the Bank of England's decision, announced in December, to widen the range of participants in its money market dealings would have a significant impact on the group's future.
The group also announced that negotiations to sell its Glasgow based equity market maker, Aitken Campbell, are at an advanced stage and that a further announcement would be made shortly.
It said that trading in the second half of the year had deteriorated and estimated an operating loss for 1996 of 1.7 million pounds. Results are due at the end of March.
Union also said it had received several unsolicited approaches over the last few weeks and added that it would be pursuing discussions with interested parties.
"The board's strategy of building fee-based businesses and withdrawing from proprietary trading ones was and is the correct one," said Union.
It added that going forward it should not only be profitable but would also have considerable unutilised assets which, if appropriate, would be returned to shareholders.

Union said that its principal continuing businesses would be Union Fund Management (UFM), its liquidity manager, and Union CAL, which is a derivatives broker and specialist in margin foreign exchange.
It added that the remaining parts of Union which have had a volatile profits record would be progressively closed down and the assets "realised in an orderly fashion."
As a result of the reorganisation it has started a a 30-day consultation procedure with employees "as a precursor to what is expected to be a substantial programme of redundancies."

It said that shareholders could be confident that, based on the balance sheet at December 31, 1996, the net assets per share will be comfortably in excess of the share price at close of business on February 24 of 86-1/2 pence.
By 0933 GMT, shares in the group had climbed 7-1/2 pence to stand at 93-1/2 pence.
